name: Templar
title: The heads of the biggest AI labs want to agree among themselves on when everyone should slow down. @TheEconomist's piece on that push ends with Covenant-72B, the model we finished training in March on GPUs contributed over the internet, as a reason such agreements may be hard to enforce. What the piece doesn't say is that once training no longer requires one giant, tightly connected cluster, the power to build new models no longer has to sit with a few companies. Globally distributed training and open models are essential tools for keeping that power from concentrating in the frontier labs. They let many more participants, from nations to companies, own a share of the future of AI and take part in building it. https://www.economist.com/international/2026/09/15/agreeing-to-make-ai-safer-may-be-impossible

name: a16z Crypto
title: RT by @a16zcrypto: a16z crypto's Eddy Lazzarin and Stanford's Dan Boneh on how AI's math leap could turn a decade of trust-building in cryptography into one month: Eddy: "We specifically rely in some sense on time... We put these schemes out and we wait. And we wait because what we believe is happening is that experts, like cryptographers and mathematicians, are testing and trying to break these things." "Because of the pace of progress on AI's mathematical abilities, there is a conspicuous absence of time... A whole new well of cognitive ability to scrutinize has appeared." Dan: "In the past, when someone would make an assumption and build a system based on it, we'd have to wait like 10 years before that system could be deployed." "Now we can just let a model run for a month, try to break it, and if the model can't break it, boy, do we have a lot of confidence that the assumption is valid." Eddy: "The labs can say, 'We took our tip-top, totally unrestricted, most cyber-capable model, and we told it to go absolutely insane, and we spent $20 million, $50 million trying to break this scheme.'" "We actually have the prospect to have more confidence in our security than ever before." @eddylazzarin @danboneh

title: "We're not afraid of hyper-intelligent bot swarms on the internet. We use them to optimise our technology." When we launched RedTeam almost two years ago we could clearly see where the internet was heading. We've since seen clients with over 90% of their traffic made up of not just automation but highly intelligent bot swarms, capable of bypassing any traditional detection mechanism. The only way to combat a threat like this is to welcome it and learn from it. By constantly ingesting and evolving attack vectors from a hive mind of miners, a Bittensor powered defence has now become the only reliable source of protection on the internet.

name: Jon Durbin
title: There are ~two economies: attention and revenue. Focus on whichever you like but if you only pick one, it probably eventually breaks. Free high intelligence = maximum attention (but probably financial/resource crisis), and conversely maximally expensive commodities restricting access rugs the attention eventually and likewise probably leads to collapse. Parallax and the new "living model" type system created out of it is perhaps a way to foster both by decreasing prices (run on phone, macbook, spark, whatever) rather than increasing them further (with larger and larger models), and ideally maintaining the intelligence (and boosting creativity/customization via this epigenesis project to prevent too much concentration into any single company/model). Ideally, everyone just brings their own resources to fund the training (sparks + apple + amd) then they own the output forever and can shape it any which way with baking in their own memory/knowledge/rules into the otherwise sparse weights after training.
